analysis.investment_thesis: ANUP is a quality niche process equipment manufacturer riding India's energy capex supercycle, with an impressive 24.5% revenue CAGR (₹245Cr → ₹733Cr) and 17.9% operating margins. However, at P/E 34.8x the PEG sits at ~1.55 using the 5Y earnings CAGR — above my comfort zone — and FY25 free cash flow turned sharply negative, signaling the story needs to prove itself before paying this price.
key_strengths: 24.5% revenue CAGR over 5 years with clear acceleration in last 3 years — a classic fast grower
17.9% operating margins are exceptional for a capital goods fabricator, showing real pricing power in niche heat exchangers and reactors
Low D/E of 0.25 with ROE of 18.9% — historically disciplined capital allocation before recent borrowing ramp
key_risks: PEG ratio ~1.55 (P/E 34.8 / 22.4% earnings CAGR) exceeds my 1.0 threshold; using the more recent 14.5% earnings growth, PEG balloons to ~2.4x
FY25 operating cash flow turned negative (-₹7Cr) against ₹118Cr net profit — massive working capital absorption that is inconsistent with reported earnings quality
Earnings growth decelerated sharply to 14.5% in FY25 (₹103Cr → ₹118Cr) even as revenue surged 35.7% — margin story showing early cracks
red_flags: FY25 FCF of -₹51Cr and OCF of -₹7Cr despite strong reported profits — divergence between earnings and cash is a classic red flag I never ignore
Borrowings exploded from ₹0 to ₹158Cr in two years while cash collapsed to ₹3Cr — the balance sheet is quietly leveraging up
Gross margin reported at 3.79% is anomalously low — suggests either a revenue recognition/pass-through materials issue or structural cost pressure worth investigating
analysis.detailed_analysis:
ANUP is exactly the kind of specialized industrial manufacturer I've always liked — a 60-year-old Ahmedabad-based niche player in process equipment (heat exchangers, reactors, pressure vessels) serving oil & gas, fertilizers, hydrogen, and pharma. The revenue growth story is real: ₹245Cr in FY20 to ₹733Cr in FY25 at a 24.5% CAGR, with operating margins expanding from ~28% to ~22% on operating income (still healthy). India's energy capex supercycle — refineries, fertilizer plants, green hydrogen — gives this company a legitimate long runway. ROE at 18.9% and D/E at 0.25 historically showed management knew how to deploy capital prudently. This is the kind of story I'd tell my wife — "they make the pressure vessels for every new refinery being built in India."

The problem is the price. At P/E 34.8x with earnings growing at ~22% historically but only 14.5% in the most recent year, the PEG is at best 1.55 and more honestly closer to 2.4x — well past where I'd feel comfortable. Worse, FY25 cash flow is a serious warning sign: the company earned ₹118Cr in net profit but generated negative ₹7Cr from operations, implying massive receivables or inventory build. FCF was -₹51Cr. Meanwhile, borrowings have jumped from zero to ₹158Cr and cash is nearly gone at ₹3Cr. This company is growing into a capex cycle and that's fine — but the current valuation prices in perfection. I'd want to see the PEG come below 1.0 (stock near ₹1,200–1,400 or earnings accelerating back above 20%+) before getting excited. Watch the next two quarters of order book execution and cash conversion closely.
